title: Replication and the replication crisis
note: A finding earns trust when independent teams can reproduce it. In the 2010s, large replication projects found that many published results, especially in psychology, did not hold up. Small samples, publication bias and flexible analyses were major causes; open science practices are the main response.

read.title: When results don't come back
text: In 2015, a team of more than 270 researchers published the results of an unusual project. They had repeated 100 experiments from respected psychology journals, following the original methods closely. Ninety-seven of the originals had reported statistically significant effects. Only about 36% of the replications did, and the effects they found were, on average, about half as large.

A single failed replication does not prove that an original finding was false; samples and settings differ. But the overall pattern pointed to problems in how research was done and published. Journals favored surprising, positive results, so null findings sat in file drawers. Small samples produced noisy estimates, and only the lucky high ones got published. Researchers could also try many analyses, drop inconvenient data, or present an after-the-fact hypothesis as if it had been predicted.

The response has been a push toward open science. Preregistration commits researchers to their hypotheses and analysis plans before seeing the data. Registered reports go further: journals review the methods and agree to publish before results exist. Sharing data and materials lets others check the work. For readers, the lesson is simple: treat one striking study as a lead, and look for independent replication.
